To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) photometric redshift accuracy can be improved by a factor of ∼2 if we include a 1.25 mm flux measurement, (ii) photometric redshifting of submillimetre sources can be improved by ∼0.1 if we include the rest‐frame FIR spectral energy distribution, (iii) photometric redshit accuracy can be improved further by ∼0 ∼1 if we include a measurement of the radio continuum flux,

photometric redshift measurements of galaxies with rest-frame FIR spectral energy distributions are possible with an accuracy of ±0,4 and that the star formation rate can be estimated with an accuracy of 20 per cent.
photometric redshift estimates can be obtained from the rest‐frame 250‐850 µ m spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of galaxies with a typical accuracy of ±0 4 and a scatter of ∼0 3.

the following questions: (i) How can the FIR/submm spectral energy distributions be used to determine photometric redshift? (ii) How does the star formation history evolve with redshift?

the following issues: (i) the derivation of the photometric redshift distribution of submillimetre sources; (ii) the derivation of photometric redshift probability distributions for individual sources; and (iii) the determination of bolometric luminosites and star formation rates from photometric redshift information.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the redshift distribution of submm galaxies is consistent with a broad distribution peaking around z ∼ 2, with the majority of the sources being at z < 3, and with some sources at lower redshift (z ∼ 1) and some at higher redshifts (z ∼ > 4).
we are not sure of what the submillimeter counts are telling us about star formation at high redshift, but the new generation of instruments will allow us to answer that question.
we have a very good idea of what the sub-millimetre sky will look like in the next few years.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
submillimetre galaxy counts and redshift distributions can be used to constrain the star formation history in the Universe.

the submillimetric spectral energy distributions of submillimetre-selected galaxies are sufficiently well defined that they can be used to determine the redshifts of these sources with a precision that is comparable to the spectroscopic redshifts.

submillimetre/millimetre photometry alone can be used to determine the star formation history and cosmic SFR density of the high-redshift Universe to an accuracy that is comparable to that obtained from deep near- and mid-infrared surveys.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the combination of submillimetre data with optical/near-IR data will allow photometric redshift estimates to be made for submillimetre selected galaxies with a precision of ∼0.4, which will be a major step forward in our understanding of the nature and redshift distribution of submillimtre galaxies.
future submillimetre/millimetre surveys will be able to provide a complete census of the star formation in galaxies over a wide range of redshifts and luminosities.
future extragalactic sub‐mm surveys have the potential of measuring the obscured star formation rate density in galaxies at all cosmic epochs.
